title: The if __name__ == "__main__" Guard
objective: Use if __name__ == "__main__": to control what runs when a file is executed directly versus imported as a module.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Full Course for free
sourceAlignment.creator: Bro Code
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only; this topic isn't covered in Python Crash Course but is taught in the companion video. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Every Python file has a built-in variable named __name__. When you run a file directly, Python sets that file's __name__ to the string "__main__". When the same file is instead imported by another file, __name__ is set to the module's own name instead.

This lets you write code that only runs when the file is executed directly, using if __name__ == "__main__":. Code inside that block runs when you run the file yourself, but is skipped when another file imports it — only the function and class definitions above it get imported, not whatever main-program code sits alongside them.

This matters because importing a module runs its top-level code once, immediately, as part of the import. Without the guard, any print() or function call sitting unprotected at the top level of a file would fire every time something imports it — usually not what you want from a file meant to be reused as a module.
explanation.rule: if __name__ == "__main__": runs its block only when the file is executed directly, never when the file is imported by something else.

examples.title: Guarding a Direct-Run Call
examples.note: Running this file directly prints the greeting, because __name__ equals "__main__" only when the file is run on its own.

examples.title: What Happens on Import (for reference)
examples.code:
# Imagine this is greeter.py:
def greet():
    print("Hello from greet()")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Only runs when greeter.py itself is executed.")

# In a different file:
# import greeter
# greeter.greet()  # works fine
# but the print() above never ran automatically on import.
examples.note: Importing greeter.py makes greet() available, but skips the guarded block entirely — that code only runs when greeter.py is executed directly. Code Forge grades a single file at a time, so this half is for reference only.

checks.question: A file is imported by another file, rather than run directly. What is __name__ set to inside the imported file?
options: The imported file's own module name (not "__main__")

feedback.correct: Correct — __name__ only equals "__main__" for the file that was run directly; an imported file gets its own module name instead.
feedback.incorrect: __name__ equals "__main__" only for the file that was executed directly — an imported file's __name__ is its module name instead.

assignment.title: Run Directly
assignment.brief: Write announce_forge() that prints 'Forge is open!', and call it only from inside an if __name__ == "__main__": guard.
requirements: Define announce_forge() that prints 'Forge is open!'.
Call announce_forge() only inside that guarded block.
assignment.starterCode:
def announce_forge():
    # Print 'Forge is open!'
    pass

# Call announce_forge() only when this file is run directly.
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    announce_forge()
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.outputCheckLabel: announce_forge() prints exactly: Forge is open!

hints: Define announce_forge() first, exactly like any other function.
Below it, on its own line, write if __name__ == "__main__":.
Indent the call to announce_forge() underneath that guard.
Since Code Forge always runs your file directly, __name__ will equal "__main__" here, so the guarded call does run.
